title: How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take? (Realistic Timeline)
meta_title: How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take? (Realistic Timeline) | American Legacy Contracting
meta_description: Wondering how long a bathroom remodel takes? Get a realistic timeline breakdown by phase, plus tips to avoid delays and minimize disruption to your home.
excerpt: Most bathroom remodels take 2-4 weeks, but major gut jobs can stretch to 6 weeks or more. Here's a realistic phase-by-phase breakdown so you know exactly what to expect.
content:
The Quick Answer

If you're short on time, here's the bottom line: most bathroom remodels take 2 to 4 weeks. A simple refresh — new vanity, fixtures, and paint — can sometimes be done in under two weeks. A full gut renovation with layout changes, new plumbing, and custom tile work typically runs 4 to 6 weeks.

But those numbers only tell part of the story. After 14 years of remodeling bathrooms across Utah County, I've learned that the real answer depends on your specific project. Let me walk you through what actually happens during a bathroom remodel and how long each phase takes.

Timeline Breakdown by Phase

Every bathroom remodel follows roughly the same sequence. Here's what each phase involves and how long you should plan for it.

Phase 1: Demo and Prep (1-3 Days)

This is where the old bathroom comes out. We remove existing fixtures, flooring, tile, and sometimes drywall. For a simple remodel, demo might take a single day. For a full gut job where we're stripping everything down to the studs, plan on 2-3 days.

This is also when we discover what's lurking behind the walls. Old homes in Payson, Spanish Fork, and surrounding areas sometimes have outdated plumbing or water damage that wasn't visible before demo. A good contractor builds contingency time into the schedule for exactly this reason.

Phase 2: Plumbing and Electrical Rough-In (2-4 Days)

If you're moving any fixtures — relocating the toilet, adding a double vanity, or changing the shower layout — the plumbing needs to be reconfigured. Electrical work happens at the same time: new circuits for heated floors, updated lighting, exhaust fan installation, and GFCI outlets.

This phase requires municipal inspections before you can move forward. In Utah County, inspection turnaround is usually 1-2 business days, but this can add time to your schedule.

Phase 3: Waterproofing (1-2 Days)

This step is critical and should never be rushed. We apply waterproof membranes to the shower area and sometimes the entire floor. Each layer needs to cure properly before tile goes on top. Cutting corners here leads to moisture damage, mold, and expensive repairs down the road.

Phase 4: Tile Work (3-7 Days)

Tile is usually the longest single phase of a bathroom remodel. The timeline depends heavily on the complexity of your design:

  • Large-format floor tile: 1-2 days
  • Subway tile shower surround: 2-3 days
  • Custom mosaic or intricate patterns: 4-7 days
  • Grout and curing time: 1-2 additional days

Tile work is an area where quality craftsmanship really shows. Rushing this phase leads to lippage (uneven tile edges), cracked grout, and a finished product that looks off.

Phase 5: Fixture Installation (1-2 Days)

Once tile is set and cured, we install the vanity, countertop, toilet, shower fixtures, mirrors, towel bars, and accessories. This phase moves relatively quickly because the heavy prep work is already done.

Phase 6: Finishing Touches (1-2 Days)

Paint, trim, caulking, final electrical connections (light fixtures, switches), door hardware, and a thorough cleanup. We also do a final walkthrough with you to make sure everything meets your expectations.

Half Bath vs. Full Bath vs. Master Bath

Not all bathroom remodels are created equal. Here's how the scope affects your timeline:

Half Bath (Powder Room)

Typical timeline: 1-2 weeks

Half baths are the simplest remodel since there's no shower or tub involved. You're usually looking at a new vanity, toilet, flooring, paint, and maybe new lighting. If you're keeping the same layout, this can sometimes be done in under a week.

Full Bathroom

Typical timeline: 2-4 weeks

A standard full bath remodel includes the shower or tub area, which adds tile work, waterproofing, and plumbing complexity. This is the most common project we do, and 3 weeks is a realistic target for most full bath renovations.

Master Bathroom

Typical timeline: 4-6 weeks

Master baths are larger and often include premium features: double vanities, walk-in showers, freestanding tubs, heated floors, and custom tile work. The bigger footprint and higher-end finishes add time to every phase.

Factors That Affect Your Timeline

Beyond the basic scope, several factors can push your timeline shorter or longer:

  • Permit requirements: Any work involving plumbing or electrical changes requires a permit in most Utah municipalities. The permit process itself can take a few days to a couple of weeks depending on your city.
  • Material availability: Custom-order tile, specialty vanities, and specific fixtures can have lead times of 2-8 weeks. We always recommend selecting materials early — ideally before demo begins.
  • Shower vs. tub: Converting a tub to a walk-in shower (or vice versa) involves more plumbing work and potentially structural changes, adding time to the project.
  • Age of the home: Older homes in the Utah County area often have galvanized pipes, outdated wiring, or non-standard framing that requires additional work once walls are opened up.
  • Scope of structural changes: Moving walls, relocating plumbing stacks, or adding windows significantly extends the timeline.

What Causes Delays (and How to Avoid Them)

After hundreds of bathroom remodels, here are the most common causes of delays I see:

  1. Material backorders: This is the number one delay. If your heart is set on a specific tile or vanity, order it as early as possible. We often recommend having all materials on-site before demo begins.
  2. Permit and inspection delays: Some municipalities are faster than others. Your contractor should know the local process and build inspection wait times into the schedule.
  3. Scope creep: "While we're at it, can we also..." is a phrase I hear on almost every project. Changes mid-project aren't necessarily bad, but they do affect the timeline. If you're considering upgrades, decide before work begins.
  4. Discovery of hidden issues: Water damage, mold, outdated plumbing — these surprises are common in older homes. A good contractor addresses them properly rather than covering them up, but it does add time.
  5. Homeowner decision delays: Tile selection, fixture choices, paint colors — having these decisions made before the project starts keeps everything moving.

Tips for Minimizing Disruption

Living through a bathroom remodel isn't fun, but these tips make it much more manageable:

  • Set up a temporary bathroom: If you're remodeling your only bathroom, coordinate with your contractor to maintain access to a toilet as long as possible. For longer projects, some homeowners set up a portable solution.
  • Order materials early: I can't stress this enough. Having tile, vanity, fixtures, and hardware ready before demo day is the single best thing you can do for your timeline.
  • Make all design decisions upfront: Create a detailed plan with your contractor covering every finish, fixture, and material before the first hammer swings.
  • Plan around your schedule: If you have a big event, holiday, or guests coming, work backward from that date with your contractor so the timeline is realistic.
  • Communicate openly: Check in regularly with your contractor. A quick daily update prevents small issues from becoming big delays.
